full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding the constraints of Part A and figuring out what kind of paper I should be looking for
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: I have an Advanced ML midsem exam Part A where I need to select a research paper from 2009-2012 from a CORE A* venue. The paper must be on ARIMA, GMM, or SVM. I am working on an automated edtech assistant project. Can you suggest a paper that aligns with my project, is easy to implement on CPU only, and will be manageable for Part C where I need to explain it without internet?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Claude gave me a concrete paper recommendation — the Mohler et al. 2011 ACL paper on short answer grading using SVM. It also explained why the paper fits my edtech project and what parts are reproducible on a laptop.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I looked up the paper on ACL Anthology (aclanthology.org/P11-1076) and confirmed it exists, was published at ACL 2011, and the authors match. ACL is listed as CORE A* on the CORE portal.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding what SVR actually does in this paper and how it differs from a standard SVM classifier
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: In the Mohler et al. 2011 paper on short answer grading, they use SVR — Support Vector Regression. Can you explain how SVR differs from SVM classification and why regression makes more sense for grading?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Explained that SVR predicts a continuous score rather than a binary class label, which is appropriate for grading because student answers exist on a spectrum rather than being simply correct or incorrect. This helped me understand a core design decision in the paper.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I verified this by re-reading the paper's methodology section which explicitly frames grading as a regression problem with scores between 0 and 5. The use of Pearson correlation and RMSE as evaluation metrics also confirms the regression framing.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Checking if the Mohler dataset is actually publicly available and how I can access it for Part B
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: Is the dataset used in Mohler et al. 2011 short answer grading paper publicly available? Where can I download it and what does it contain?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Claude confirmed the dataset (Texas A&M CS short answer dataset) is publicly available and described its structure — around 2273 student answers across 80 questions from a Data Structures course, with scores from two human annotators.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I searched for the Mohler dataset online and found references to it in multiple NLP and EdTech papers that cite it as a benchmark. The dataset has been used in subsequent ASAG research which confirms it is accessible.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding failure cases and limitations of this approach so I can speak confidently in Part C
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: What are the main failure cases or limitations of using SVM with text similarity features for automatic short answer grading as done in Mohler et al. 2011? When would this approach break down?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Helped me think about failure modes I had not considered — like paraphrasing that preserves meaning but changes surface form, domain-specific jargon the similarity metrics do not capture, and the fact that the model is trained on a single course so it may not generalize.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: The paper itself acknowledges that lexical similarity measures fail when students use valid synonyms or rephrase answers in creative but correct ways. I also cross-checked this with my understanding of cosine similarity's limitations from our lecture on text representation.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Planning a simplified but faithful implementation for Part B that runs on my laptop without any GPU
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: For Part B of my exam I need to reproduce results from Mohler et al. 2011 on a standard laptop with no GPU. What is the simplest faithful reproduction I can do using scikit-learn? What features should I prioritize?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Suggested a practical roadmap: use TF-IDF cosine similarity as the main feature, optionally add WordNet path similarity, feed into scikit-learn SVR, and evaluate using RMSE and Pearson correlation. This is exactly what I plan to implement.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I verified that scikit-learn's SVR and TfidfVectorizer are well documented and CPU-friendly. I also checked that NLTK's WordNet interface works without any paid API, which I confirmed from the NLTK documentation.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding the dependency graph alignment component of the paper and whether I need to implement it
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: The Mohler 2011 paper uses dependency graph alignments as one of its contributions. How complex is this to implement and do I need to fully reproduce it for a student-level Part B submission?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Claude clarified that the dependency graph alignment is the more novel contribution but also the most complex to implement. It suggested that a simplified version using just the similarity features and SVR already demonstrates the core ML contribution and is defensible for Part B.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I re-read the paper's ablation-style results and noticed that even without graph alignment, the similarity-only SVM model performs reasonably well. This confirms that a partial reproduction is academically valid.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding kernel choice assumptions in SVR for text similarity features
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: In Mohler et al. 2011, SVR is used with text similarity features for short answer grading. What assumptions does the choice of kernel function (linear vs RBF) make about the feature space? For a small dataset of ~2000 student answers with similarity-based features, which kernel would generalize better and why?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Clarified that a linear kernel assumes features are already in a space where classes are linearly separable, which is reasonable for normalized similarity scores. RBF would add flexibility but risks overfitting on ~2000 samples. This shaped my plan to start with a linear kernel in Part B.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: I verified this by reviewing the SVR documentation in scikit-learn and recalling from our SVM lectures that kernel choice is a bias-variance decision. The paper does not explicitly state which kernel was used, so this is something I need to investigate during reproduction.

full_llm_interaction_log.purpose: Understanding how C and epsilon hyperparameters affect SVR generalization on a small grading dataset
full_llm_interaction_log.prompt: SVR has two key hyperparameters: C (regularization) and epsilon (insensitive tube width). In the context of grading student answers where training data is limited to one course, how do C and epsilon affect the bias-variance trade-off? What would overfitting look like in this grading task specifically?
full_llm_interaction_log.how_it_helped: Understood that a high C forces SVR to fit training grades very tightly, risking poor generalization to unseen student phrasings. Epsilon controls how much deviation from the true score is tolerated — too small and the model memorizes minor phrasing differences. This directly informs my hyperparameter tuning plan for Part B.
full_llm_interaction_log.student_verification: Verified against our lecture notes on SVM regularization. The concept of the insensitive tube is covered in Vapnik's original SVR formulation which I cross-checked in the course reading material.
